source.title: A Blessing of Dimensionality in Membership Inference through Regularization
source.authors: Jasper Tan; Daniel LeJeune; Blake Mason; Hamid Javadi; Richard Baraniuk

record.tranche_reason: Its own width, epoch, and feature-count sweeps report test or validation error trends that bear on the proposed double-descent shapes; the reported trends do not show the predicted rise and peak.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior double-descent results, which are not rows. Test-error sweeps are recorded below; membership-inference advantage results are omitted because they do not measure the claim's test-error behavior. Validation-error and test-error trends used to select or describe model settings are included only where the paper reports a sweep result.
record.test_reason: The study is about membership inference, but it reports its own test- or validation-error sweeps over NN width (Fig. 3), training epochs (Fig. 4), SVM feature count (Fig. 14) and bi-level logistic-regression overparameterization φ (Fig. 3, theory). These bear on V1, V2, V4 and V6 in a new setting. It does not argue that any version is wrong, so T3 fits better than T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find that width and training trade test error against membership-inference vulnerability, and that larger models paired with tuned regularization (early stopping or ridge) improve both. They take generalization gains with width as given from the double-descent literature rather than testing double descent.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies membership-inference vulnerability and privacy–utility trade-offs, with test-error sweeps over width, epochs, and feature count; it does not reproduce the original double-descent method or measure the interpolation threshold.
record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS 2023), PMLR Volume 206
record.problems: The test-error trends are presented mainly in figures without extractable numeric values. The width experiments use validation-selected early stopping, and the paper does not report training error or identify the interpolation threshold for these sweeps.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant test-error sweeps left out. Membership-advantage results in Figures 3–14 are omitted because they do not measure the claim's test-error behavior.

untested.parts: Interpolation threshold and training error are not reported, and there is no training-to-convergence width sweep.
Label-noise settings and the location of epoch-wise interpolation are not tested.
The classical U-shape below interpolation is not shown, and the threshold is not marked.
Label noise as the driver of the peak, multiple peaks, and an untuned-versus-tuned comparison are not tested.
Not tested. Effective parameters are mentioned only as future work.

missing.what: Test-error vs width and vs epochs repeated in global-loss-threshold runs (separate shadow/target models); same monotone trends.
Theoretical test error vs ridge strength 1/λδ for several φ (regularization dependence of error).

record.verdict_notes: All trend values are figure-only. Because the width sweeps use optimal early stopping, the absence of a V1 peak is not a clean challenge; Nakkiran et al. themselves report that the peak attenuates under early stopping. In the SVM sweeps, regularization switches from C=1 to hard margin at p=n, which confounds the threshold region.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not report the training-set fitting threshold or establish whether a peak is located where the model just fits the training set.
The paper does not establish an epoch corresponding to interpolation or relate any peak location to training-set fit.
Training sample size is not swept to measure test error near an interpolation threshold.
The sweeps do not establish the interpolation location or comprehensively test the curve across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location.
The paper does not test whether label noise or variance drives a double-descent peak, whether peaks split, or whether optimal regularization removes such a peak.
The paper does not re-express complexity using an effective parameter count or test whether that changes the curve to an ordinary U shape.

relation.reason: The study reports generalization error versus width, epochs, and SVM feature count, together with theoretical logistic-regression results; these directly bear on the claim versions.

tranche.reason: Its own error sweeps bear on the claims in a membership-inference setting, although double descent is not its primary research question.

source_check.notes: Figure-only values are appropriately left unquantified. The authors study privacy–utility trade-offs; the record should distinguish their own error sweeps from a controlled demonstration of double-descent peak removal.

statements.correction: Figure 3: Purchase100 two-layer NN, CIFAR10 ResNet18, Multi30K Transformer; checkpoints selected by maximum validation accuracy; test error decreases with width; no paired demonstration of an unregularized peak being removed; interpolation thresholds not identified.
statements.problem: The study reports decreasing error under validation-selected early stopping, but does not demonstrate removal of previously reported peaks or locate interpolation in these sweeps.

statements.correction: R4: Purchase100 two-layer NN; R5: CIFAR10 ResNet18 with random translations and horizontal flips; R6: Multi30K English-to-German Transformer. Figure 4 and Section 3.2: test error decreases with epochs and can subsequently remain constant. No label-noise threshold is established by this study.
statements.problem: The no-rise observation is supported, but the listed datasets and architectures do not describe all three cited rows from this study. Its Purchase100 and Multi30K results are omitted from the conditions.
